what.title: What it is
what.body: SkyBlink shows images from the SPHEREx mission of the same patch of sky over time, to find objects that move or change in brightness, and shows their spectrum.
what.origin: Made for NASA Space Apps 2026. It is an independent project: it is not a NASA product and does not imply NASA's endorsement.

ai.title: Use of artificial intelligence
ai.body: SkyBlink's code was written with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic), under the team's direction and review.

spherex.name: SPHEREx
spherex.body: Images from the SPHEREx mission (NASA/JPL-Caltech), from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). NASA public data.

surveys.name: 2MASS and WISE (AllWISE)
surveys.body: Surveys funded by NASA (2MASS also by the NSF), from the IRSA archive. Public data.

dss.name: Digitized Sky Survey (DSS)
dss.body: Photographic plates from the MAST archive at STScI. They are not in the public domain: license CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, for scientific, educational and non-profit use; commercial use is prohibited. The copyright holder depends on the plate (Caltech/Palomar, AURA/STScI, UK SERC/PPARC and the Anglo-Australian Observatory) and is shown below each one.

sky.name: Star map on the sphere
sky.body: NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio, “Deep Star Maps 2020”. Gaia DR2: ESA/Gaia/DPAC. It is visible light, not a SPHEREx image.

constellations.name: Constellations and stars on the sphere
constellations.body: Figures, constellation names and star names from d3-celestial, by Olaf Frohn (BSD 3-Clause license). Boundaries from the table by Nancy Roman (1987), taken from astropy (BSD 3-Clause license).

names.name: Object names
names.body: SIMBAD and Sesame, from the CDS (Strasbourg).

code.name: Code
code.body: The code is MIT licensed; the data keep the licenses above.

sound.title: About the sound
sound.body: “Listen to the spectrum” does not play the sound of the object: space does not carry sound and these data are light. It is a way of hearing the chart: it sweeps the spectrum from the shortest wavelength to the longest in {{seconds}} seconds; at each moment, more flux sounds higher (up to {{octaves}} octaves above {{hz}} Hz) and slightly louder, and where there is no data there is silence.
